name: Maquista / Macao Creole Portuguese
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 10 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Senna Fernandes, Miguel & Alan Norman Baxter. 2004. Maquista Chapado: vocabulary and expressions in Macao's Portuguese Creole. Macao: Instituto Cultural do Governo da Região Administrativa Especial de Macau. ISBN 99937-0-069-X. (archive.org item maquista-chapado-1, CamScanner scan, 114 pp.)
catalog_locator: Introduction, sec. 5.3 'Main syllable stress and the written accents used in the orthography of this vocabulary', pp. xviii-xix, and sec. 5.4 'The phonetic representation of compounds and phrasal expressions', pp. xix-xx.
catalog_quote: Most Maquista words have a stressed penultimate syllable, as in Portuguese. Exceptions to this rule are indicated by a written accent. To this effect, the (^) and (´) accents are used. In the present work these written accents have the following values: The circumflex accent (^) indicates a closed stressed e, a or o vowel, in any position in the word: ôlo ['olu] eye, abolô [abo'lo] lacquered box, comê [ko'me] eat, bêzo ['bezu] kiss, falâ [fa'la] speak, pônto ['pontu] bridge, sâm [saŋ] being. The acute accent (´) indicates the principal stressed syllable in the following cases: (i) on the vowels e, a, and o, it indicates a (semi-) open vowel, for instance: mulé [mu'lɛ] woman, wife; nuncassá [nuŋka'sa] it is not needed; corasám [kɔra'saŋ] heart; (ii) on stressed i and u vowels in word final position, for instance: izizí [izi'zi] to demand. Both the circumflex accent (^) and the acute accent (´), when placed on a vowel that is followed by a nasal consonant, besides indicating the tonic syllable of polysyllables, and the degree of openness of the vowel, have the additional function of indicating that the vowel is not nasalized: vêm [veŋ] to come, pám [paŋ] bread, coraçám [kɔra'saŋ] heart.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is lexical, Portuguese-style: the default and majority pattern is penultimate stress; a large lexically specified class is stressed on the final syllable (all verbs, which end in a stressed vowel after loss of -r: falâ, comê, abrí, izizí; nouns in -ám < Ptg. -ão such as coraçám; mulé < mulher), and these non-penultimate cases are marked with a written accent in the orthography.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No word-internal secondary stress described. Sec. 5.4 (pp. xviii-xix): in compounds and phrasal lexical expressions 'the last main stress in a sequence of words [is] the strongest while the main stresses on the previous words become secondary or are neutralized', treated as an intonation effect dependent on speech rate.
new_statements.exceptions: Exceptions to penultimate stress are marked orthographically (circumflex for closed stressed vowels, acute for open stressed vowels and for final stressed i/u); footnote: in most words ending in -ám the stressed /a/ varies between semi-open and open (except sâm 'be'). Authors caution (sec. 5) that without acoustic analysis they avoid detailed phonological claims.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns citation-form words as transcribed in the vocabulary (each word 'transcribed as a unit with its own stress weight'); phrase-level strengthening of the last stress noted separately. Variety: traditional Maquista of Macao, based on recordings of elderly speakers in Hong Kong and Macao (1980s) and Batalha's 1950s-80s material.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes 'Maquista' = Macau Creole Portuguese / Patuá macaense (maca1262), traditional variety of Macao as recorded from elderly speakers in Macao and the Hong Kong diaspora (1980s recordings by J.-M. Charpentier, plus Batalha's material); not Macau Pidgin Portuguese (a separate Glottolog entry).

sources.locator: Introduction, section 5.3 'Main syllable stress and the written accents used in the orthography of this vocabulary', p. xviii (continuing to p. xix, sec. 5.4)
sources.note: Introduction sec. 5 'Phonetic transcription', 5.3 'Main syllable stress and the written accents', p. xviii: most Maquista words have penultimate stress as in Portuguese; exceptions marked by written accent (circumflex = closed stressed e/a/o, e.g. comê [ko'me], falâ [fa'la]; acute = (semi-)open stressed vowel or stressed final i/u, e.g. mulé, coraçám, izizí). Sec. 5.4 (pp. xviii-xix): in compounds/phrasal expressions the last main stress of the sequence is strongest, earlier ones become secondary or neutralized. Sec. 5.1: minimal vowel reduction in unstressed syllables.

Tertiary: says phonology is similar to European Portuguese with a 'sing-songy quality'; circumflex/acute accents in the orthography indicate syllable stress and vowel openness. No positional rule; cites Batalha, Ferreira, Senna Fernandes & Baxter.

sources.note: 'Fonética > Acentos' p. 11: acute/circumflex accents used very frequently because vowels are very open or closed and because verbs never end in -r but in a stressed vowel (botá, comê, abrí, discompô), 'obrigando assim a acentuação da vogal tónica'. No positional stress rule stated.
